He pointed out that the construction industry has a "rainy season" arrangement in response to typhoons and heavy rain, allowing construction schedules to be postponed, and that extremely hot weather should also be taken into consideration, suggesting the Government could take the lead in following up. He also suggested that the Government should adjust the standards for the "Work Heat Stress Warning" for outdoor work, and advocated for severe penalties against non-compliant employers.

Extremely hot weather has once again put the outdoor working environment under the spotlight, and the "occupational safety hard man" feels it most keenly. Ho Ping-tak, who has been in the scaffolding industry for many years, has various views on scaffolding. The Government has recently expressed its intention to introduce metal scaffolding. Under extremely hot weather, what is the most obvious difference between metal scaffolding and bamboo scaffolding in terms of temperature, and just how big is the difference?

Site metal scaffolding - "can easily reach over 60, or even 70 degrees"

Ho Ping-tak said that generally speaking, the metal scaffolding used at construction sites uses iron tube frames, which are heavier than the aluminium tube frames used for small-scale maintenance works, and transfer heat faster. An iron tube waiting to be installed, placed in direct sunlight without any shade, "can easily reach over 60, or even 70 degrees".

Witnessed seven workers at a construction site, five suffered from heatstroke

Ho Ping-tak once visited a metal scaffolding site and stood on the roof using a thermometer to measure the temperature - it showed 54.6 degrees. He had also visited a site on Anderson Road in Kwun Tong, where five of seven workers on the ground showed signs of heatstroke. He added that metal scaffolding absorbs far more heat than traditional bamboo scaffolding, and the level of hardship correspondingly increases in extremely hot weather.

Sites provide ice cream and fruits to cool down - Ho Ping-tak: Only large-scale sites have this. Ho Ping-tak pointed out that although some sites now install thermometers or wind speed display screens around the premises, and some companies even provide ice cream, fruits and herbal tea to cool down, giving people the impression that the working environment is gradually improving, such benefits are limited to large-scale sites. Very few companies proactively offer workers rest after the Labour Department issues a "Work Heat Stress Warning". In reality, workers still have to "figure things out themselves", such as bringing their own neck fans, fan jackets, or using large water bottles to make ice pellets to bring back to the site.

He mentioned that when the Labour Department established the "Work Heat Stress Warning" in 2023, frontline workers were very happy, saying "the Labour Department has finally spoken up to fight for this heat warning for us frontline workers." He said workers had originally expected this warning to allow sites to temporarily halt work like typhoon or rainstorm warnings, but "over 200 warnings have been issued, and none have reached the red level requiring work stoppage." What is even more absurd is that during the earlier "record-breaking high temperatures", only a yellow warning was issued.

Ho Ping-tak pointed out that temperatures vary between Central, construction sites and hillsides. Although he is not a professional, he questioned whether the mechanism for issuing Work Heat Stress Warnings should be adjusted to address the situation of outdoor work. "Some construction sites reach over 50 degrees, so when so-called experts formulate measures, shouldn't they experience it for themselves? Not just sit in an air-conditioned room looking at data. I believe that for any theory, to prove whether it works, practice is what matters most."

Rainy season allows construction extensions - Ho advocates for the Government to take the lead and treat extremely hot weather equally

Ho Ping-tak further pointed out that many companies in the industry have a concept of "rainy season", meaning that after work stoppages due to typhoons or heavy rain, companies can be granted extensions to delivery deadlines. He explained that this practice exists because in the past Hong Kong might have had five or six typhoons a year, and in severe weather "bamboo would slip, and the tie wires would come loose." But for extremely hot weather, workers similarly feel dizzy, yet there is currently no similar consideration. If construction deadlines are imminent, "it's too hot to rest, but the construction period doesn't change, the concrete pouring schedule doesn't change, so many brothers and co-workers are actually very helpless."

He believes that the current heat stress warning is in a situation where "following it is a favour, not following it is also reasonable", because construction delays would incur daily penalty charges. When employers calculate the numbers and find that "they can't catch up with the developer's penalties even if they work themselves to death", they will naturally choose to exploit workers, putting workers in a passive position. He suggested the Government consider making rest periods under the warning mandatory, and imposing penalties on main contractors who fail to comply. The Government should also take the lead by extending construction periods during extremely hot weather without penalty, so that main contractors would follow suit.

Lai Tung-kwok, a Legislative Council member from the Hong Kong Federation of Trade Unions, also agreed that even if the threshold for issuing heat stress warnings were revised, "I still doubt whether it would be red every day? Perhaps on the hottest days it would only be eight or ten days," and he believed the impact on overall construction would be limited.
